_about: Canned model behaviour for Cwoffee's automated tests. Nothing here is a claim
about what a real model would say: it is the shape of a response, chosen so the
wire path (SSE parsing, tool-call fragmentation, JSON repair, telemetry from
`timings`, streaming block commit) is exercised without a GPU and without
Selection is stateless on purpose: a scenario is the first entry whose `match`
substring appears in the last user message, and the step played is the number of
role=tool messages after that user message. A tool loop therefore advances by
itself, which also proves the prompt builder really is append-only: every request
is a superset of the previous one.
$path in a tool argument expands to the last path-shaped token of the matching
user message, so the harness can interpolate its own temp paths into a prompt and
the canned tool call still names the right file.

scenarios._why: a long four-paragraph answer with real structure: this is the turn the frame-cadence and follow checks ride on
scenarios.match: Write about coffee roasting in exactly four paragraphs

steps.content:
## Roasting coffee at home

Roasting is the point where green coffee stops being a shelf-stable seed and becomes a flavour. A cheap pan, a colander and a stove hood will do it; what matters is that the beans move constantly and that you can hear the two cracks.

The first crack is steam. The beans have given up their moisture, the cell walls let go with a sound like popcorn, and the coffee is drinkable from here on - light, acidic, and tasting of wherever it grew.

Then comes Maillard browning, which is where sweetness is made. Heat drives sugars and amino acids together; body thickens, acidity softens, and the origin's sharper notes start to blur behind roast taste.

Second crack is structure failing. Oils surface, the beans swell and go brittle, and every minute past it trades origin for char. Stop when the cup says stop, not when the timer does.

What makes it different from filter coffee is pressure: nine bar forces water through a compacted puck in under thirty seconds, extracting compounds that gravity brewing cannot reach, and it produces crema, which is the only part of the cup that is genuinely unique to the method. Crema is not a mark of quality by itself - it is largely a product of fresh CO2 and bean roast date, and it dissipates within minutes - but a thin, quickly-vanishing crema usually correlates with a stale coffee or under-extraction. The rest of the shot is dissolved solids, in roughly an eight to twelve percent concentration band; anything lower reads thin, anything higher reads hollow, and the whole craft is choosing where inside that band you want your bitterness and your acidity to sit. There is also a thermodynamic argument for espresso, which is that a small volume of liquid near boiling will lose heat quickly, so the cup must be small, and the smallness in turn constrains the dose, which constrains the grind, and so the machine sets the recipe more than any roaster or barista does, which is why people who brew at home tend to arrive at espresso last and complain about it loudest.\nEOF"}
